About me

I approach most things the same way - find out what it is, understand how it works, then do it step by step. If I get stuck, I try every possible route before asking for help. That's not stubbornness, it's just how I learn best.

I can get interested in almost anything, as long as it seems interesting or something that makes me wonder. I have a habit of always opening the comment section, scrolling through it, and then searching for whatever caught my eye. One fact leads to the next, and that is how I learn. It's also how I found Power BI and SQL. After working with Python in one internship, I kept coming across them, so I looked them up, watched tutorials and built a project.

The same curiosity took me into internships in Data Science & Analytics, Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning, Content Writing, Email Marketing and Data Analytics. None of it was planned, all of it was curiosity.

I don't try to learn everything at once; I prefer figuring things out one step at a time. But when something matters, I give it everything, going deep enough to understand it properly. I work best independently within a clear framework, so I know what I'm doing and what I'm accountable for.

Banking & Compliance

Why does my bank keep asking? KYC and AML in plain language

How this started

I kept hearing the same phrase, "complete your KYC." The bank said it. The gas agency said it. Each time I did it without really knowing what it was or why it mattered. After a Foundation in AML and KYC course, I wanted to explain it the way I wish someone had explained it to me.

The question

What exactly are KYC, CDD and AML, and what do banks do with them behind the counter? How is a customer identified, how is information verified, what happens when something does not match, and how does KYC fit into the wider fight against money laundering?

KYC, CDD and AML: what is the difference?

KYCCDDAML
What it isKnow Your Customer: checking who you are and where you liveCustomer Due Diligence: understanding what kind of customer you are and how risky the relationship isAnti-Money Laundering: rules and checks that stop crime money looking honest
The questionWho are you?What kind of customer are you?Is this money behaving normally?
WhenAt the start, refreshed over timeAt the start, deeper for higher riskAll the time
Looks atDocuments, address and photoWork, source of money, ownership, risk levelTransactions and patterns
ExampleOpening a savings account, buying a SIM card, getting a gas connectionTracing the real owners of a company before opening its accountFlagging many deposits just under a limit

Think of a building: KYC checks your ID at the gate, CDD asks why you are visiting and how much access you need, and AML is the CCTV watching afterwards. CDD gets deeper as risk rises, with enhanced checks for higher-risk customers such as politically exposed persons (people in senior public roles). Laundering itself usually moves in three stages: placement, layering and integration.

The KYC lifecycle

1Identify→2Collect documents→3Verify→4Due diligence→5Ongoing review

Four questions I wanted answered

Question 1: How does a bank decide you are who you say you are?
  • Documents: ID proof, address proof and a photo.
  • Matching: details are checked against records, through Aadhaar-based verification or Video KYC, where an official checks you live on camera.
  • Risk rating: customers are placed into risk levels, and higher-risk ones get more checks.
Question 2: Why does my bank keep asking for the same documents?
  • KYC is not one-time. Banks must keep records current, re-verifying at intervals that depend on your risk level.
  • Your name, address or phone number may have changed, or a document may have expired.
  • Each institution has its own legal duty, so your bank, mutual fund and gas agency cannot rely on each other's checks.

It is annoying, but it makes it harder for someone to misuse your identity.

Question 3: What happens when a large cash deposit walks into a bank?

Take "Asha" (a made-up customer), a teacher who deposits a large sum in cash. That is not a crime, but it does not match her usual pattern, so the bank may ask where the money came from, such as a land sale or a family gift. Cash transactions above a set limit are reported to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-IND) as routine, and anything suspicious, at any amount, is reported as a suspicious transaction, which the customer is not told about.

Warning signs: deposits split to stay under a limit, many unrelated people paying into one account, a suddenly busy account, or lending your account for a commission (a "money mule").

Question 4: What happens when something doesn't match?

A mismatch is not automatically fraud. It means the information must be reviewed under the organisation's procedure. Scenario: a customer's name is spelt slightly differently across documents, and the address on the form does not match the supporting document.

Identify the discrepancies → Review the documents → Clarify with the customer → Re-check the updated information → Escalate if unresolved → Document what was done.

Bonus: when the customer is a company

The review traces who owns and controls the company to find the beneficial owner, the real person who ultimately owns or controls it: company → ownership and control → owners and controllers → verification and risk review.

My KYC review checklist
  • Customer information is complete
  • Required documents are available
  • Information is consistent across documents
  • Relevant information can be verified
  • Risk indicators are considered
  • Discrepancies are reviewed, not assumed
  • Actions and outcomes are documented
  • Cases needing review are escalated

What I learned

KYC is not simply "checking an ID." It is a structured process of identification, verification, due diligence, documentation and ongoing review. It also connected something I had already done elsewhere, checking information carefully and documenting what I found, with a business process where that discipline matters a great deal.

What I'm still unsure about

Rules and limits change and differ between institutions. I hold a foundation certificate and I am not a compliance officer, so this explains the ideas and is not advice.

Under the hood

  • Terms: KYC, CDD, AML, PMLA 2002, RBI KYC Master Direction, FIU-IND, CKYC.
  • Certificate: Foundation in AML and KYC (KYC Lookup).

Banking Analytics

Where does a bank's money actually move?

How this started

After my AI & ML internship, which was one of the toughest things I had done as someone from a non-tech background, I wanted to learn more tools like it. I kept hearing about Power BI and SQL, so I taught myself the basics on YouTube and tried building something real.

The question

Banks record thousands of transactions a day. If you tidy that raw record, what does it say about how customers use their money?

What made it hard

Everything was new. I got stuck on how to use KPIs and slicers and what to build with them, made plenty of mistakes, and corrected the dashboard many times.

How I tackled it

  1. Cleaned and checked the data in Excel so I could trust the numbers.
  2. Wrote 7 SQL queries, each answering one question, such as who spends most and where.
  3. Built the Power BI dashboard with 8 charts and 2 slicers so a reader can filter it themselves.
  4. Fixed my mistakes and added colour until it was easy to read.

Side by side

Deposits

53%

of total transaction value

Everything else

47%

of total transaction value

What I found

  • More than half of all money moving (53%) was deposits.
  • Chennai and Lucknow had the highest transaction value.
  • Customers with car loans kept the highest average balances.
  • Savings accounts made up about 60% of customers.

What it gave me

It is a beginner-level project, but it showed me my own effort, and it proved I could learn new tools on my own. That confidence mattered most. I would love to build a better version someday.

What I'm still unsure about

This is one dataset of 2,000 transactions, so the patterns may not hold for a much larger bank.

Under the hood

  • Excel for exploring and validating the data.
  • 7 SQL queries run in SQLite (SELECT, GROUP BY, COUNT, AVG, SUM) for customer segments, spend patterns, loan risk and monthly trends.
  • Power BI dashboard with 8 charts and 2 slicers.

Data analytics

Which used cars keep their value?

How this started

This was a guided, hands-on analysis in my VOIS for Tech Data Analytics internship, built to show how a real analysis moves from raw listings to clear patterns.

The question

If you were buying a second-hand car, which kind would still be worth the most when you sell it?

How I tackled it

  1. Loaded 299 CarDekho listings into Python and checked what was in them.
  2. Added two columns of my own: the car's age and how much of its price it had lost.
  3. Grouped the cars by fuel type, gearbox and age and compared the averages.
  4. Turned the differences into charts and a dashboard.

Side by side

Diesel

₹10.10L

average resale value

Petrol

₹3.26L

average resale value

What I found

  • Diesel cars sold for about three times what petrol cars did (₹10.10L against ₹3.26L).
  • Automatics sold for more than double manuals.
  • CNG cars seemed to lose the most value (about 49%), but there were only a couple of CNG cars in the data, so I would not rely on that.
  • Cars older than 12 years lost much more of their price.

What it gave me

It made me comfortable with Python and its libraries, and I can now do a few analyses like this on my own.

What I'm still unsure about

Diesel cars may simply be bigger, pricier models to begin with, so fuel type is probably not the only reason. 299 listings is also a small slice of the market, and CNG, with just a couple of cars, is the weakest result.

Under the hood

  • Python with pandas, numpy, matplotlib and seaborn in Google Colab.
  • Exploratory data analysis, with derived columns for car age and depreciation %.
  • Part of the VOIS for Tech Data Analytics programme (Edunet Foundation).

Research report

Do brands that listen keep their customers?

How this started

I found this topic through another academic project. I came across a research paper on Google Scholar, read it, and found it so interesting that I proposed it to my mentor, and she approved it. It taught me things I had heard of but never paid attention to until I started learning them.

The question

Brands now use AI to read reviews and comments. Does responding to what customers say make them more loyal?

What made it hard

A tight deadline left little time to collect real opinions, and I was studying for mid-semester exams while also getting feedback and making changes.

How I tackled it

  1. Built the report mainly around one key research paper.
  2. Added journals, blogs and company case studies from the internet.
  3. Ran a short survey of simple questions with friends, classmates and working professionals (family members and their colleagues).
  4. Compared what the research said with what my small survey showed, then wrote it up with my mentor's feedback.

Side by side

Published research

Positive

Studies I read link responsive, personalised brands to more engagement

My survey

Mostly agreed

From people I know, so small and friendly

What I found

  • Most survey respondents said brands that respond to feedback earn more of their trust.
  • The published research I read points the same way.
  • Personalised and quick replies were the features people mentioned most.

What it gave me

It taught me to read research, build an argument from sources, and be honest about what a small sample can and cannot show.

What I'm still unsure about

The survey was small and came mostly from people I know, who may answer more kindly than strangers. It asked about AI in general, not sentiment analysis specifically, so it shows opinions, not proof.

Under the hood

  • Secondary research plus a Google Forms survey with Likert-scale questions.
  • Responses analysed with Excel and AI tools; basic percentages only, no statistical tests.
  • What I learned: a report is only as strong as its sources, and small samples need careful wording.
Secondary researchGoogle FormsExcel

Data analytics

Which farming season pays best, and which wastes water?

How this started

This was the major project of my VOIS for Tech Data Analytics internship, and the one I submitted with a presentation. The brief was to find patterns in how Indian farms perform across seasons.

The question

Indian farming runs in three seasons: Kharif, Rabi and Zaid. Does the season change how much a farm grows, earns and spends on water?

How I tackled it

  1. Explored the 4,000-record dataset in Excel first, then moved to Python.
  2. Compared Kharif, Rabi and Zaid on yield, profit, water use and disease risk.
  3. Looked at which crops and irrigation methods drove the differences.
  4. Put the findings into a dashboard and presented them.

Side by side

Kharif

Profit

the most productive and profitable season

Zaid (summer)

Loss

averaged losses

What I found

  • Kharif was the most productive and profitable season; Zaid (summer) averaged losses.
  • Sugarcane out-yielded every other crop by a wide margin.
  • Sugarcane and chilli earned the highest average profit, while wheat, rice and maize averaged losses.
  • Rain-fed farming used water most efficiently; drip was best among managed irrigation.
  • Disease and pest risk clustered between about 30% and 65% on most farms.

What it gave me

It made me comfortable with Python and its libraries, and I can now do a few analyses like this on my own.

What I'm still unsure about

These are averages and patterns, not proof of cause. Weather, soil and crop choice are tangled together.

Under the hood

  • Python (pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn) in Google Colab; Excel for first exploration.
  • 4,000 records, 28 variables; yield, profit, water-efficiency and disease-risk comparisons by season, crop and irrigation method.
